objectives: Write a clear request and checks for an AI coding agent.
Predict what the agent will change before it starts.
Read the change and spot anything you did not ask for.
Test the result, report a problem and retest after the fix.
Explain what running a website as a service takes.
outcomes: Spec: given the starter page and a one-sentence need, each learner writes a plain-English change request that names the one change, who it helps and two things that must stay the same, plus three acceptance checks in the form I do this, I expect that. A partner can run every check without asking what it means.

Prediction: before the agent runs, each learner writes which part of the page (HTML, CSS or JavaScript) the change needs and one thing that could break, then compares the prediction with the agent's plan and names one match or difference.

Review: given the before-and-after view of the agent's change (slide 10 or the projector), each learner marks every changed line as asked for or not asked for and finds the one change that breaks a requirement, with no more than one prompt.

Testing: at their own workstation, each learner runs the five checklist tests (happy path, no match, mixed case, keyboard, narrow screen) on the agent's version, records expected, actual and pass or fail, writes a repair request with steps, expected and actual, and after the repair reruns the failed check and two checks that passed before.

SaaS: using the resource finder as the example, each learner explains at least four of these six with a reason: where it would be hosted, why visitors sign in (authentication), where saved data lives, where a private API key goes, what it costs, and who maintains it.
agenda: Warm-up and reconnect

Reconnect: two learners share the practice step they chose at the end of week 5. Recall: in week 1 you let AutoCorrect change teh to the and checked it before keeping it; in week 5 you kept passwords private. Today a much bigger automatic helper changes a web page, and both rules still apply. Pairs discuss slide 2: where would a wrong change hurt most?
Introduction: goals and the example

Read the goals on slide 1 aloud. Slide 3 in one minute: SaaS is software you use in a browser while a company runs it. Play chapter 1 (0:00–0:46). Every learner opens slide 9 and selects Open starter app: this is version 1, the page the agent will change. Name the loop on the board: spec, plan, change, review, test, revise.
Cycle A: spec and acceptance checks

Tell: slides 4, 6 and 7 (agent, prompt, spec, acceptance check). Show: chapter 4 (pause at 2:52 so learners can write), then chapter 5 (3:00–3:44); build the class spec live with the slide 7 builder. Do: worksheet tasks 1 and 2, every learner writes their own spec and three checks. Review: a partner reads each check aloud and says whether they could run it without guessing; pick one learner's checks for the demo.
Cycle B: predict, then read the plan

Tell: slides 5 and 8 (HTML, CSS and JavaScript; ask the agent for a plan first). Show: chapter 3 (1:32–2:14); after the predictions, give the class spec to the AI coding agent on the projector in plan mode and read its plan aloud. Do: worksheet task 3, every learner writes a prediction before the plan appears, then compares. Review: show of hands for HTML, CSS or JavaScript; approve the plan only if it matches the spec.
Cycle C: the agent changes, you review

Tell: slides 11 and 10 (one change at a time; a diff shows removed lines with a minus sign and added lines with a plus sign). Show: approve the plan, let the agent make the change, then show the before-and-after on the projector; chapter 6 (3:44–4:01) shows keeping a working version first. If the live run is slow or fails, use the prepared version on slide 10. Do: worksheet task 4, every learner marks each changed line on slide 10 as asked for or not asked for. Review: partners compare; ask which change nobody asked for and which check would catch it.
Break
Screen-free pause. Leave version 1 and the worksheet open.
Cycle D: test with the checklist

Tell: slide 17 (happy path, no match, mixed case, keyboard, narrow screen). Show: chapter 7 (4:27–5:11) and chapter 8 (5:11–5:55), then test the live agent's page on the projector while the class calls out each check. Do: worksheet task 5, every learner opens the agent's version (resource-finder-agent.html) at their own seat and records expected, actual and pass or fail in the App test log. Review: the slide 20 knowledge check; a learner who found a failing check reads out their evidence.
Cycle E: repair and retest

Tell: slides 18 and 12 (regression; a repair request names the steps, expected, actual and what to keep). Show: chapter 9 (pause at 6:37), then paste one learner's repair request into the agent and read its one-line diff together. Do: worksheet tasks 6 and 7, every learner writes a repair request, then opens the repaired version (resource-finder-agent-fixed.html) and repeats the failed check and two checks that passed before. Review: a partner confirms that nothing that passed before now fails.
Cycle F: what makes it SaaS

Tell: slides 3, 13, 14, 15 and 19 (SaaS, where data lives, API key, authentication, hosting, cost and upkeep). Show: chapter 2 (0:46–1:32) and chapter 10 (6:44–7:31), then press Ctrl and U on the agent's page to show that anyone can read a page's code. Do: worksheet task 8, every learner fills in the SaaS table for the finder. Review: the slide 21 knowledge check; two learners each explain one trade-off.
Individual check

Each learner shows you three things: one acceptance check and its result, the change the spec did not ask for, and one SaaS trade-off with a reason. Score the extension rubric (0, 1 or 2 per row) and mark Independent, With prompt or Needs practice on the roster; re-model only the missing step.
Apply and close

Slides 22 to 24. Home task: choose one website you already use that runs as a service, such as web email. Write where your data lives, how you sign in, and one check you would run after the company changes the site. Keep it with your worksheet. Then select Start fresh on this computer at each station.
lab: Write a change request (a spec) for the agent in plain English. The need: visitors type a kind of help, like learning, not a name. Say the one change, who it helps, and two things that must stay the same. The slide 7 builder can make a first draft.
Write three acceptance checks in the form I type or press this, I expect to see that. Make one check about the new change and one about something that already works and must not break.

Before the agent runs, predict: which part will it change (HTML, CSS or JavaScript), about how many lines, and one thing that could break. Then read the agent's plan on the projector and write one way it matches or differs from your prediction.

Open slide 10 and read the agent's change (the diff). A line with a minus sign was removed; a line with a plus sign was added. Mark each changed line asked for or not asked for, and write down the change that breaks what the spec said to keep.

Open the agent's version (resource-finder-agent.html) at your own seat. Run the five checks in the App test log: happy path (learning, then library), no match (zzz), mixed case (LIBRARY, then Learning), keyboard only, and narrow screen (zoom to 400%). Record expected, actual and pass or fail.
Write a repair request the agent could act on: the steps, what you expected, what actually happened, and what must stay the same.
Open the repaired version (resource-finder-agent-fixed.html). Repeat the check that failed, then two checks that passed before. Record the results and say whether you accept the repair.

Suppose the finder became a SaaS website where many people save favorite resources. Write where it would be hosted, why visitors would sign in, where saved favorites would live, where a private API key for a map service would go, and what it would cost and who would keep it running.
answers: One change: the search box also finds resources by category, so learning shows every Learning resource. Who: a visitor who knows the kind of help but not the name. Must stay the same (any two): capital and small letters match alike (LIBRARY finds Community library); the no-match message; keyboard use; the narrow-screen layout; only resource-finder.html changes; no outside code, personal data or sign-in. A strong spec also asks for a plan first.

For example: I type learning, I expect Community library and Practice Workbook Workshop (2 fictional resources found). I type LIBRARY, I expect Community library (1 found). I type zzz, I expect No matching resources. Try a different word or reset the filters. Accept any checks a partner can run without guessing.

JavaScript, the rule that decides which resources match (one or two lines), and perhaps the hint text in the search box (HTML). Could break: capital-letter matching, the no-match message or the Category list. A good plan names resource-finder.html only and the matching rule. Accept any reasoned prediction; the comparison matters more than being right.

Asked for: the search also looks at the category (r.category added). Not asked for but harmless: the hint now says Try library or learning. Not asked for and harmful: .toLowerCase() was removed from the line that reads the search box, so capital letters no longer match. Learners may say it in plain words: it stopped ignoring capital letters.

Version 2 results: learning, 2 fictional resources found (Community library, Practice Workbook Workshop), pass. library, 1 found (Community library), pass. zzz, No matching resources. Try a different word or reset the filters., pass. LIBRARY and Learning, No matching resources instead of 1 and 2 found, fail (a regression: version 1 finds LIBRARY). Keyboard: Tab reaches the link, search box, Category and Reset filters, each with a thick outline, pass. Narrow screen at 400%: one column, no sideways scrolling, pass; the round Text size button can cover part of the page in every version, which is a course issue, not the agent's change.

Steps: open resource-finder-agent.html and type LIBRARY. Expected: Community library (1 found), as in version 1. Actual: No matching resources; Learning also finds nothing while learning finds 2. Request: make capital and small letters match the same resources again; keep the new category search and everything else the same; show the change before applying it.

LIBRARY: 1 found (Community library), pass. Learning: 2 found, pass. Passed before and still pass: learning (2 found), library (1 found), zzz (no-match message), keyboard outline. Accept the repair because the failed check now passes and no earlier check broke. If the instructor's live repair differs, it is retested the same way.

Hosted: on a web server or hosting service so anyone with the address can use it (today it is one file on the course site with fixed data). Sign-in: so each person sees only their own favorites; the server must check it, because a sign-in picture is not security. Saved data: in a database on the server, not in this page or one browser. API key: on the server only, since anyone can read a page's code with Ctrl and U. Cost and upkeep: hosting, web address, map service and AI agent fees; someone must update listings, fix problems, back up data, help users and review every agent change. Accept four of six with a reason.

slide_changes.title: Solve one small problem
slide_changes.body: Our fictional resource finder works. Visitors want to type a kind of help, like learning, and see every match. Today an AI coding agent makes that change. You decide what to ask for, check what it did and test it.

slide_changes.title: Website, web app, and SaaS
slide_changes.body: A website shows pages. A web app responds when you type or click. SaaS (software as a service) is software you use in a browser while a company hosts it, keeps the data, secures it and updates it, usually for a fee.

slide_changes.title: Vibe coding starts with clear instructions
slide_changes.body: An AI coding agent is a program that reads your files, plans a change, edits the code and can run checks, all from a plain-English request. The loop: spec, plan, change, review, test, revise. You approve each step and own the result.

slide_changes.title: Three parts of a browser app
slide_changes.body: HTML is the content and structure. CSS is the look and layout. JavaScript is the behavior, such as deciding which resources match a search. Before the agent starts, predict which part our change needs.

slide_changes.title: Write acceptance checks first
slide_changes.body: An acceptance check is a test anyone can run: I type or press this, I expect to see that. Write them before the agent starts. Include one check for the new change and one for something that must keep working.
items: Write three I do, I expect checks
Add one check that must not break

slide_changes.title: A prompt with useful boundaries
slide_changes.body: A prompt is what you type to the agent. A spec is a careful prompt: Let the search box also find resources by category. Keep capital-letter matching, the no-match message and keyboard use. Change only this file. Show your plan first.

slide_changes.title: Ask the AI to explain its work
slide_changes.body: Before the agent edits anything, ask for its plan: which file, what it will change and how it will check the result. Compare the plan with your spec and your prediction. Approve it only when they match.

slide_changes.title: Start with a working reference
slide_changes.body: This is version 1, before the agent. Open the starter app and run three quick checks: library, LIBRARY and zzz. Keep this version as the way back if a change goes wrong.

slide_changes.title: No AI account? You can still build
slide_changes.body: A diff shows exactly what changed. A line with a minus sign was removed; a line with a plus sign was added. You need no AI account to review one. Mark each changed line: asked for, or not asked for?

slide_changes.title: Make one change at a time
slide_changes.body: Keep version 1. Ask for one change. Read the diff. Run every check. If a check fails, ask for a repair or go back to version 1.

slide_changes.title: A useful revision request
slide_changes.body: LIBRARY and Learning now find nothing, but library and learning work. Make capital and small letters match the same resources again. Keep the new category search and everything else the same.

slide_changes.title: Where does the data live?
slide_changes.body: In our finder, the resource list lives inside the page file. Browser storage keeps data in one browser on one computer, and it can be cleared. A SaaS keeps shared data in a database on its server, behind sign-in and access rules.

slide_changes.title: Keep secrets out of browser code
slide_changes.body: An API key is a secret code that lets your app use another company's service, such as maps, and bills you for it. Anyone can read a page's code (Ctrl and U), so private keys stay on the server.

slide_changes.title: A mock sign-in is not security
slide_changes.body: Authentication means proving who you are, usually by signing in. A sign-in box drawn on a page protects nothing. A real SaaS checks who you are on its server, then decides what each person may see.

slide_changes.title: Watch: prompt, test, revise
slide_changes.body: Play one chapter at a time as your instructor directs. Pause at 2:52 to write checks and at 6:37 to write a repair request. Replay any chapter; captions and a transcript are available.

slide_changes.title: Test more than the happy path
slide_changes.body: The happy path is the normal use you expect to work. Also test no match (zzz), mixed case (LIBRARY, Learning), keyboard only and a narrow screen. Record expected, actual and pass or fail.

slide_changes.title: Fix what you can demonstrate
slide_changes.body: A regression is something that used to work and broke after a change. Report the steps, what you expected and what happened. After the repair, repeat the failed check and two checks that passed before.

slide_changes.title: Hosting is a separate decision
slide_changes.body: Hosting means putting the page on a web server so anyone with the address can use it. Running it as a service also means costs, backups, updates, support and a person who reviews every agent change.

slide_changes.title: Knowledge check: AI confidence
slide_changes.body: The agent reports: Done. All checks pass. What should you do next?
options: Accept it, since the agent ran the checks
Read the change and run our checks yourself
Ask the agent to confirm the checks again
slide_changes.why: An agent's report is a claim, not evidence. Read the diff and run the acceptance checks on the saved page yourself. Asking again only repeats the claim.

slide_changes.title: Knowledge check: a secret key
slide_changes.body: Your finder will show a map from a paid service that needs a private API key. Where should the key go?
options: In a hidden comment in the page
On the server, never in the page
slide_changes.why: Anyone can open a page's code, including comments and script files. A private key stays on the server, which calls the map service for the page. Some services also give public keys made for browsers.

slide_changes.title: Lab: build, test, explain
slide_changes.body: Show your partner your spec, your checks, the change nobody asked for, your test log and your retest. Explain one thing a real SaaS version would need.

slide_changes.title: You can direct a build and judge it
slide_changes.body: Keep the loop: spec, plan, change, review, test, revise. Tools will change. Clear requests, careful review and your own tests stay useful.

prep: Each station: Microsoft Edge, headphones, this lesson and worksheet (typed, or printed for anyone who prefers paper), and Notepad as the plain-text editor for the optional hand repair. Learners need no account and no AI access: they open three practice pages on the course site, resource-finder.html (version 1), resource-finder-agent.html (version 2, the prepared agent result with one planted defect) and resource-finder-agent-fixed.html (version 3). At the front: your own computer on the projector with an AI coding agent signed in to your account, a practice folder holding copies of resource-finder.html and resource-finder-agent.html under version control, the terminal text enlarged, and the agent set to ask before every edit. Never show a sign-in page, key or bill on screen. Rehearse the whole demo with the class spec the week before and record it as a backup; the prepared pages are the fallback if the agent is slow, offline or does something unexpected. Print slide 10's diff and the App test log for anyone who wants paper. Play video chapters 4, 7 and 9 with captions to check sound. After your run-through, select Start fresh on this computer at each station. No paid service, purchase or learner account is required.
lab_paths: Put two pages side by side

Press Ctrl and N to open a second Edge window and open the other version there. Press the Windows logo key and the Left arrow, then choose the other window for the right side. Or hover over the Maximize button and pick a layout.
See a page's code
Press Ctrl and U. The code opens in a new tab; you can read it but not change it. Close that tab when you are done.
Find a word on a page or in its code
Press Ctrl and F and type the word. Matches are highlighted. Press Ctrl and G to jump to the next one.
Reload a page
Press F5, or Ctrl and R.
Test with the keyboard only

Press Tab to move to the next control and Shift and Tab to go back. Each control should show a thick outline. On Category, press the Up or Down arrow to change the choice. On Reset filters, press Enter.
Test a narrow screen
Press Ctrl and + until the zoom reaches 400%. The page should become one column you can read without scrolling sideways. Press Ctrl and 0 to go back to 100%.
Show file name extensions
In File Explorer, select View › Show › File name extensions. Names now end in .html or .txt, so you can spot a wrong save.
Find a downloaded file
Press Ctrl and J to open Downloads in Edge. Downloaded files are in the Downloads folder in File Explorer.
Open an HTML file in Notepad
In File Explorer, right-click the file, select Open with, then Notepad. If Notepad is not listed, select Choose another app.
Save a web page from Notepad
Choose File › Save as. Type a name ending in .html. Set Save as type to All files, then select Save. Or type the whole name in quotation marks, such as "resource-finder-v3.html".

instructor_notes: Rehearse the exact demo the week before with the tool you will use (for example, Claude Code). Put the practice folder under git so git diff shows the change and git restore gives you a way back. Record the rehearsal as a backup video.

Keep the agent from acting on its own. In Claude Code, recent versions start in auto mode: start with claude --permission-mode plan, read the plan aloud, then approve with 'Yes, manually approve edits' so each edit waits for you. Press Esc to stop it at any time.

A live agent is unpredictable. If it gets the change right, say so, then switch to the prepared version: 'Another run of the same request produced this one.' If it is slow, fails or wanders, stop it and use slide 10 and the prepared pages; nothing in the lesson depends on the live run.

Keep learners in the thinking seat. They write the spec and checks before they see the agent's plan, and they test at their own seat. Do not let the agent's 'all checks pass' stand in for their tests; that is slide 20's point.

Never show a sign-in page, key or bill on the projector, and enlarge the terminal font before class. Write these terms on the board and point to each as it comes up: agent, prompt, spec, acceptance check, happy path, diff, regression, hosting, SaaS, API key, authentication.
